newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Cautious UK budget leaves open EMU option.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Cautious UK budget leaves open EMU option.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's budget gives Britain the option of joining Europe's Economic and Monetary Union in 1998, a Reuters survey of economists showed on Wednesday.

With an eye on meeting convergence criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, the blueprint for a single currency, the chancellor produced a prudent budget on Tuesday, analysts contributing to a post-budget survey said.

"Basically Clarke is a Europhile and he wants the UK to be a part of the European single currency and monetary union. The budget does not risk the ability to meet the deficit criteria," said Olwen Renowden, economist at Sakura Finance.
Thirty-five economists took part in the survey, which asked for forecasts for interest rates and gilt yields.
They expect base rates, now six percent, to rise to around 6.50 percent by mid-1997 and around seven percent by end-1997.
Ten-year gilt yields are expected to rise from around 7.49 percent now and stabilise around 7.9 percent from mid- to end-1997.
One of the conditions that must be met for a country to qualify for EMU is a 1997 budget deficit that is three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP).
In early November the European Commission forecast the British budget deficit at 4.6 percent of GDP for 1996 and 3.5 percent for 1997.
Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS, calculates an overall fiscal tightening of about one billion sterling and agrees the chancellor wanted to keep his options open.

"The market had expected a neutral to a slightly inflationary budget. But even if you strip out the optimistic assumptions the Treasury made, the overall fiscal stance is neutral to slightly tight," he said.

Clarke raised the GDP growth forecast for 1997 to 3.5 percent from 3.25 percent. The prediction for the public sector borrowing requirement was reduced to 19 billion sterling for fiscal 1997/98 starting April 6 from 23 billion sterling.
But he left the target for core inflation unchanged at 2.5 percent.
Of the 35 economists surveyed, 33 based their forecasts on the assumption that the opposition Labour party would win a majority in the election, which has to be held by next May.
Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, assumed the Conservative government would win a fifth term.
Sakura's Renowden assumed no clear victor in the election and based her forecasts on a Labour-controlled coalition.
"If Clarke was to lead the Conservatives in the election after this one, it would be on a European ticket," she said.
